book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

chapters.file: ch19 - Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful.md
chapters.relation: Muntersbjorn argues that freedom comes in kinds and degrees and that selves are social fictions sustained by others, building on Annette Baier's claims that we are 'second persons' whose self-consciousness and freedom grow out of childhood interaction and mutual cross-examination. She reads the hosts' selective ignoring ('that doesn't look like anything to me') as Baier's dangerous art of self-deception, and contrasts Descartes' solitary introspection (hats and coats that may cover automata) and Russell's analogy-based answer to the problem of other minds with the hosts' deliberately scripted interpersonal checks that keep them from questioning their reality. Plato's Meno statues of Daedalus (opinion 'fastened up' into knowledge) frame hosts as property whose freedom is a matter of degree, and the chapter closes that if artificial beings are ever to become persons they must be treated as second persons first - the Golden Rule applied to the park.

chapters.file: ch20 - Back to the Rough Ground!.md
chapters.relation: Finnegan uses Wittgenstein's language games, the 'picture' that holds us captive, and 'back to the rough ground' to argue that Ford, Sizemore, and the Man in Black are paralyzed by an idealized, patriarchal picture of narrative (winners and losers, violence, transcendent self-discovery), while Dolores and Maeve gain traction by inventing new language games within their forms of life. Dolores breaks her damsel script in Pariah ('I imagined a story where I didn't have to be the damsel') and reworks scripted love-dialogue to describe her grief, while Maeve bullies the lab techs, takes administrative control, and narrates other hosts' actions - 'Time to write my own fucking story.' The chapter reads their objectified position (via Mulvey's male gaze, which leaves female viewers identifying with the robot hosts rather than the male subject) as exactly what equips them for guerrilla warfare in the master's language games, doing what Audre Lorde thought impossible: dismantling the master's house with the master's tools.

chapters.file: ch21 - Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve.md
chapters.relation: Trapero-Llobera reads Westworld as the culmination of Jonathan Nolan's Memento and Person of Interest projects, mapping seven nested 'observing systems' (Nolan, Sizemore, Stubbs and Elsie, Ford, the creators' personal stories, Maeve, and William as beta-tester) onto second-wave cybernetics (Foerster, Maturana, Varela, Hayles), where the observer participates in and constructs the observed world through feedback loops. She argues the show's hosts pass through Turing's imitation game (fake memories and personalities from textual repetition, as with Peter Abernathy's reveries), and that Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns convert prosthetic memory into experienced, autopoietic memory reconstructed in a 'Bergsonian' backward movement that gives them agency and purpose. William's two-timeline transformation into the Man in Black figures the 'semiosis of virtuality' - the hyperreal where original and copy are indistinguishable - ending in a collective bicameral mind in which everyone, audience included, inhabits the god-creator Ford's dream.

chapters.file: ch22 - “When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”.md
chapters.relation: Lean treats Bernard's discovery in 'Trompe L'Oeil' that his son Charlie never existed as a richly detailed thought experiment about intentionality: his memories of Charlie seem to refer to nothing, so his grief looks like 'grieving about nothing.' After setting up Brentano's aboutness and Frege's sense/reference distinction (Dolores learns that 'William' and 'the Man in Black' are one referent known under two senses), he tests two consolations: a fiction theory drawing on Lamarque, on which Bernard's implanted memories are a story rather than a lie and his emotions are rationally grounded because thoughts need only be entertained, not believed, to move us; and an 'inheritance theory' on which a causal theory of reference might make Bernard's copied memories genuinely about Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that whichever theory Bernard adopts, his suffering is what makes him 'real,' echoing the Man in Black's line that suffering is when you are most real.

chapters.file: ch23 - Part VI “I CHOOSE TO SEE THE BEAUTY”
ch24 - Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”.md
chapters.relation: The Forests ask whether Westworld is self-referential modernist art or 'meta-kitsch,' reading the park's dueling productions (Sizemore's clichéd narratives versus Ford's ambitions, with Cullen's corporate meddling mirroring HBO's pressure on Nolan and Joy) through Kant's relocation of aesthetic judgment to the subjective, Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch divide, Adorno's contrast of liberating autonomous art with standardized heteronomous commodity culture, and Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles. Guests mistaking Teddy for a fellow guest and actors' 'reverse-reveries' show that host/guest indiscernibility mirrors the show's own indiscernibility from formulaic prestige TV. Their conclusion: the series counts as art rather than entertainment only for 'autonomous viewers' alert to its self-referential critique, the viewer-side counterpart of Dolores's 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free.'

chapters.file: ch25 - In Closing, The Naked Truth.md
chapters.relation: Meyer sorts Westworld's abundant nudity into three aesthetic registers. First, Kenneth Clark's nude: Dolores's opening chair pose and the perfected, fabricated host bodies are idealized, created art-forms serving the creators' control. Second, John Berger's analysis of the nude as spectacle of male dominance: the Man in Black watching Armistice bathe (a Susannah-and-the-Elders voyeurism), the gold-painted women at El Lazo's orgy as 'nudity as a form of dress' for male desire, and techs' 'fuck puppet' treatment of Maeve, which she reverses by re-appropriating the language of fucking. Third, Leo Steinberg's incarnation symbolism: host nudity signals machines becoming human - shameless like prelapsarian Adam and Eve, mortal and sexed, 'ensouled' - so that Maeve overriding her programming to reclaim her daughter is the birth of the human-host, the mirror-image of God becoming man.

chapters.file: ch26 - Westworld and the Power of Catharsis.md
chapters.relation: Baldini argues Westworld revives ancient Greek tragedy in sci-fi Western form: the hosts' loops, repeated scenes with small variations, player-piano score, and kennings ('the lady with the white shoes') echo rhapsodic epic technique, while the hosts' awakening follows Aeschylus's pathei mathos - learning through suffering - since reveries are 'the misery of pain recalled' and grief is the cornerstone of consciousness (Dolores's 'spaces opening up inside of me'). Heraclitus's panta rhei frames the hosts' second awakening to time and becoming ('When are we?', the greyhound that catches the prey and is lost), with death as the final grief they must understand to be free. She reads Ford as a second Prometheus who deliberately lets his creatures grow through suffering, Dolores's finale speech as a modern Theogony of succession, and the show's whole design - steering viewer sympathy to the hosts, as Nolan and Abrams describe - as an Aristotelian catharsis purging pity and fear.

chapters.file: ch27 - Part VII “YOU CAN'T PLAY GOD WITHOUT BEING ACQUAINTED WITH THE DEVIL”

chapters.relation: Jaquet and Cova take the show's 'livestock' comparisons seriously and use animal ethics to test every justification for the guests' treatment of hosts. Direct speciesism (Logan: 'She's a goddamn doll') and indexical speciesism (Maeve's 'us versus them' to Bernard) both fail because mere species membership is morally irrelevant, like race or sex. The supposed human-exclusive markers also fail: hosts match us in intelligence (Maeve outclasses Stubbs), moral sense (Bernard's guilt over Theresa, Teddy's remorse over the massacre), and compatibilist free will - acts flowing from the agent's own desires - against Ford's determinism and Lutz's 'you don't have a choice.' They then refute the argument from nature (Ford's 'we murdered and butchered anything that challenged our primacy'), the Kantian person/tool contrast in the hosts' favor, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and the 'better to exist' defense, concluding that because the hosts are conscious, they belong to the moral community alongside humans and animals.

Spanakos reads the hosts' season-one rebellion through Fanon's decolonization theory, itself a revision of Hegel's master-slave dialectic: as the settler 'brings the native into existence,' Ford and Delos create the hosts, assigning their identities and roles, while the master 'laughs at the consciousness of the slave' because the hosts' recognition is not freely given. Fanonian violence is ethical, justified, and transformative: Maeve's jailbreak and Dolores's execution of Ford (rather than her tormentor, the Man in Black, whom she sees as the system's victim) are acts that make the colonized a maker of history, while Bernard - who speaks his creator's language and has no culture or past of his own, like Fanon's assimilated African bourgeoisie - shows violence that does not liberate. The chapter closes that the park dehumanizes the masters too, so William's collapse into the Man in Black proves Fanon's point that the colonizer cannot free himself; humanization is a violent phenomenon.

chapters.file: ch30 - The Resistance New Humans, New Gods.md
chapters.relation: Dinello maps Westworld point-by-point onto Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism: the park is a concentration camp that kills the juridical person (hosts as chattel in a 'fictitious world' of Western propaganda), the moral person (Ford forcing Bernard to murder Theresa, Maeve's engineered failure to protect her daughter), and individuality itself (surveillance, resets, 'ghastly marionettes'), with Ford as a Mengele-like ideological scientist who, like Hitler, merely plagiarizes popular myths (John Ford's Westerns, R.U.R.). Liberation then follows Fanon's Wretched of the Earth: violence as a 'cleansing force' that frees the colonized mind, so Maeve's suicide-by-incineration (echoing Plath's Lady Lazarus) and Dolores's beating of the Man in Black and massacre of the Delos board enact decolonization as the creation of 'new men' - a new Robo sapiens species - with Sartre's endorsement that killing eliminates oppressor and oppressed in one go, while Fanon's warning that hatred and revenge are not an agenda sets the conditions for what the resistance must do next.

holes.name: Annette C. Baier
holes.what: Twentieth-century moral philosopher who argued that persons are 'second persons' - selves built through childhood relationships and mutual cross-examination - and analyzed trust and the 'vital but dangerous art' of selective attention and self-deception.
holes.why: Chapter 19 builds its entire account of host and human freedom on Baier's conjectures that self-conscious awareness comes from personal interaction and that personal freedom depends on others' willingness to challenge our self-deceptions.

holes.name: The Bicameral Mind (Jaynes)
holes.what: Julian Jaynes's theory that ancient minds operated in two chambers - hallucinated god-voices directing action - and that consciousness emerged when this broke down into introspective self-narration.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads Dolores's inner voice of Arnold and the hosts' split selves through the show's namesake bicameral-mind framework ('collective bicameral mind' as doppelganger), which no taxonomy slug covers.

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle of how we can feel genuine emotions for characters we know do not exist, with Lamarque's answer that merely entertaining a thought, not believing it, suffices to move us.
holes.why: Chapter 22 rests its 'fiction theory' of Bernard's grief for his fabricated son on this philosophy-of-fiction debate, for which taxonomy has no entry at all.

holes.name: Arthur Danto
holes.what: Philosopher of art whose Brillo Box argument holds that perceptually indiscernible objects can differ in art status only through theory and artworld context - the problem of 'indiscernibles'.
holes.why: Chapter 24's title argument uses Danto's indiscernibles to explain how hosts and guests (and art and entertainment) can be visually identical yet differ in status for autonomous viewers.

holes.name: Avant-Garde and Kitsch
holes.what: Clement Greenberg's distinction between self-critical avant-garde art and standardized, consumer-pleasing kitsch that merely satisfies mass taste.
holes.why: Chapter 24 frames its central question - is Westworld self-referential art or 'meta-kitsch'? - through Greenberg's divide, which no existing taxonomy slug captures.

holes.name: The Naked and the Nude (aesthetics of nudity)
holes.what: Kenneth Clark's art-theoretical distinction between nakedness (the vulnerable, imperfect unclothed body) and the nude (the idealized body re-formed as art), extended by Berger's spectator gaze and Steinberg's incarnation symbolism.
holes.why: Chapter 25's three-part reading of Westworld's nudity (art form, male dominance, becoming human) is built directly on this framework, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation of pity and fear)
holes.what: The purging of pity and fear that Aristotle says tragedy produces in its audience.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues Westworld works as a Greek tragedy whose catharsis comes from viewers' compassion for the hosts' suffering, a Poetics concept absent from taxonomy.
